result.question: What doubling interval and cost trend does the slide give for transistor count under Moore's Law?
result.answer: Based on the provided sources, the transistor count doubles roughly every two years (or every 18–24 months), with a minimal increase in cost.

retrieved_chunks.text: MOORE’S LAW • The mathematical model: • If transistor count doubles every T years: • Where:N0 = initial transistor count • N(t) = transistor count after time t • T = doubling period • t = elapsed time • For Moore's Law: T=2 years

CLASS ACTIVITY • "If a computer has 5 billion transistors today,how many could it have after 10 years if the transistor count doubles every 2 years?“ Moore’s Law • Moore’s Law is the prediction that the number of transistors on a chip will double roughly every two years, with a minimal increase in cost. • Moore’s Law, created by Gordon Moore before he co-founded Intel, has remained the golden rule for the electronics industry since its 1965 publication. • Moore’s Law only stops when innovation stops, and innovation continues to push forward.

INTEGRATED CIRCUIT LOGIC TECHNOLOGY • Historically, transistor density increased by about 35% per year, quadrupling somewhat over four years. • Increases in die size are less predictable and slower,ranging from 10% to 20% per year. • The combined effect was a traditional growth rate in transistor count on a chip of about 40%–55% per year,or doubling every 18–24 months. • This trend is popularly known as Moore’s Law.

CLASS ACTIVITY • 1. A processor currently contains 4 billion transistors. Assuming Moore's Law,estimate the transistor count after 6 years. • 2. A CPU has 10 billion transistors. Another CPU has 80 billion transistors. Assuming Moore's Law, approximately how much time separates the two generations?
EXERCISE • A chip currently contains 3 billion transistors. Under a two-year doubling rate, after how many years would it theoretically exceed 100 billion transistors?
